title: The Big Bang
text: Around 13.8 billion years ago, the universe began expanding from an unimaginably hot, dense state. Within minutes it had forged the nuclei of hydrogen and helium. Nearly all the hydrogen in your brain is that old.

title: First Stars and Heavy Elements
text: Within a few hundred million years, the first stars lit up the darkness. Inside them, and in their explosive deaths, hydrogen and helium were fused into carbon, oxygen, nitrogen and more. We are, quite literally, made of star stuff.

title: Formation of the Earth
text: About 4.54 billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust collapsed to form the Sun and its planets. Young Earth was molten and battered, yet it held the ingredients and, eventually, the oceans that life would need.

title: Oceans and Prebiotic Chemistry
text: As Earth cooled, oceans formed, and simple molecules may have begun to combine into amino acids, nucleotides and fatty lipids. Lipids naturally curl into bubbles, tiny compartments that would one day wrap every living cell.

title: First Single-Celled Life
text: By 3.5 billion years ago, and probably much earlier, the first living cells had appeared. They were single cells, but they could already sense chemicals and respond. That is the seed of every nervous system.

title: Chemical Signalling
text: Early cells learned to read their world with receptor proteins that catch specific molecules. A signal arriving outside sets off a chain reaction inside. Neurons still communicate using this ancient chemical language.

title: Ion Channels and Membrane Potential
text: Cells learned to pump charged ions across their membranes, building up a voltage like a tiny battery. Channel proteins that open and close that flow are the same machinery that fires every nerve impulse in your brain today.

title: Bacterial Chemotaxis
text: Bacteria evolved a tiny sense-and-act loop. Receptors compare chemical levels over time, and the cell adjusts its spinning flagella to swim toward food and away from poison. It is a brainless decision, and a blueprint for reflexes.

title: Eukaryotic Cells
text: Around 2 billion years ago, one cell swallowed another and the two became partners. The swallowed bacterium became the mitochondrion, a power plant that fueled bigger and more complex cells, including eventually neurons.

title: Multicellular Life
text: Over a billion years ago, cells began sticking together and sharing the work. Multicellular bodies need coordination, and that need would eventually give rise to nerves. Our closest single-celled cousins, the choanoflagellates, already carry many genes later used in synapses.

title: Sponges: Animals Without Neurons
text: Sponges are some of the oldest animals alive. They have no neurons at all, yet their cells still signal each other with chemicals and calcium waves. They stand at the edge of the story, just before the first nerve cells.

title: First Neurons and the Nerve Net
text: Around 600 million years ago, some animals began using cells that carry electrical signals. In jellyfish and sea anemones they form a nerve net, a web of neurons with no central command: the first step toward every brain that followed.

title: Bilateral Symmetry and Ganglia
text: Animals that crawl or swim in one direction developed a head end and a tail end, with matching left and right sides. Their neurons began to gather into clusters called ganglia, connected by nerve cords. Centralizing the nervous system made faster and smarter responses possible.

title: Cephalization: The First Heads
text: As animals moved forward through the world, their senses and neurons piled up at the front. This process is called cephalization, and it created the first heads. The cluster of neurons in a head is what we now call a brain.

title: The Cambrian Explosion and the Rise of Eyes
text: About 540 million years ago, animal life diversified dramatically in the Cambrian explosion. Many animals evolved eyes, and the race between hunters and hunted favored sharper senses. Processing all that visual information pushed brains to become more complex.

title: Chordates: Notochord and Dorsal Nerve Cord
text: Chordates added a stiff rod called the notochord and a hollow nerve cord along the back. That nerve cord is the forerunner of our spinal cord and brain. It also helped these animals swim with coordinated, wave-like movements.

title: The First Vertebrates
text: Around 520 million years ago, the first true vertebrates swam in Cambrian seas. They had a head with paired eyes and a protective braincase, built by new embryonic cells called the neural crest. These innovations let the brain grow more complex.

title: The Tripartite Brain
text: Early vertebrates organized their brains into three parts: the forebrain, the midbrain and the hindbrain. Each part took on different jobs, from smell and vision to balance and breathing. Your own brain still follows this ancient three-part plan.

title: Dopamine as a Learning Signal
text: Early in vertebrate history, neurons that release dopamine took on a special job. They fire when things turn out better than expected and fall silent when worse. That teaching signal lets an animal learn which actions lead to good outcomes.

title: Lampreys: Camera Eyes and an Old Brain Plan
text: Lampreys are living jawless fishes that preserve a very old vertebrate brain design. They have a camera-style eye and the same basic brain layout we have. Studying them shows that this plan arose before jaws did.

title: Basal Ganglia: Actor and Critic
text: Deep in the forebrain, the basal ganglia pick the next action. Dopamine adjusts how strongly each choice is favored, based on how well it turned out. Scientists often compare this to an actor choosing and a critic judging, and the circuit appears in lampreys.

title: Jawed Fishes and Myelin
text: Jawed fishes appeared and spread, and with them came myelin, a fatty wrapping around nerve fibers. Myelin makes signals travel much faster and more efficiently. Fast nerves were a big advantage for large, active predators.

title: The Pallium in the Fish Forebrain
text: The roof of the vertebrate forebrain is called the pallium. In fishes it handles smell, learning and memory. Much later, in mammals, a part of it would swell into the cerebral cortex.

title: Tetrapods Move onto Land
text: About 375 million years ago, fishes like Tiktaalik, with sturdy fins and lungs, were exploring the shallows, and their relatives became the first animals with four limbs. Life in air demanded new ways to see, hear and move.

title: Amniotes: Life Free from Water
text: Amniotes evolved eggs that could survive on land, freeing animals from needing water to reproduce. They spread across dry habitats and soon divided into the reptile and mammal lineages. Their forebrains began to develop the layered structures that would later become the cortex.

title: Synapsids: Our Branch Splits Off
text: Around 315 million years ago, our own branch of the tree began: the synapsids split from the line leading to reptiles and birds. Their brains were small, but held the pallium tissue that would one day become the neocortex.

title: The Reptile Brain Plan
text: Reptiles evolved a compact brain with strong brainstem, midbrain and basal ganglia circuits for movement, habit and survival, under a thin layered cortex. We still carry these structures, and reptile brains turn out to be more capable than once believed.

title: Cynodonts and the Road to Warm-bloodedness
text: Cynodonts were among the first synapsids to look and act a bit like mammals. As their bodies learned to stay warm, their nervous systems could work faster and for longer. Energy-hungry brains finally had a steady power supply.

title: Early Mammals Take the Night Shift
text: Imagine a creature the size of a shrew, hiding from dinosaurs by day. At night it hunts by smell, sound, and whiskers. Those senses expanded the brain regions that would become the heart of the mammalian mind.

title: The Six-Layered Neocortex Appears
text: Only mammals have a neocortex, a thin sheet of neurons stacked in six layers. The same circuit pattern repeats across the sheet. Make the sheet bigger and you get new abilities, which is exactly what happened later.

title: Three Tiny Bones Sharpen Hearing
text: Three tiny bones in your middle ear began as part of the jaw. Their move into the skull made hearing sharper, especially for high-pitched sounds. The brain gained a richer acoustic world to analyze.

title: Limbic System and Hippocampus Take Shape
text: Memory, emotion, and bonding came together in the limbic system. The hippocampus builds maps of places and stores events. Together with feelings, this let mammals learn quickly and care for their young.

title: Imagining Paths: Replay in the Hippocampus
text: A rat at a fork in a maze sometimes stops and looks both ways. In its hippocampus, cells fire in sequence as if it were walking down each path. This looks like a simple form of imagining, and it lets mammals try options before acting.

title: Agranular Prefrontal Cortex and Mental Simulation
text: Early mammals developed frontal cortex that connects the new neocortex to the older brain systems for emotion and action. It may have decided when to imagine, and which imagined outcomes were worth acting on. This is a hypothesis, and it is still being tested.

title: Dinosaurs Fall and Mammals Radiate
text: When the dinosaurs vanished, mammals inherited the Earth. They spread into new habitats and lifestyles, and at first their bodies grew faster than their brains. Bigger brains followed millions of years later.

title: The First Primates Climb into the Trees
text: Early primates lived in the trees. Grasping branches and leaping between them called for careful vision and fine touch. The brain started to devote more tissue to hands and eyes.

title: Forward-Facing Eyes and a Visual Brain
text: Two eyes facing forward give two slightly different views of the same scene. The brain compares them to see depth. A large visual cortex grew to process all of this, and vision became the main primate sense.

title: Trichromatic Color Vision
text: A small gene duplication gave our ancestors a third kind of color receptor. Suddenly ripe fruit stood out from leaves. The brain gained a new color channel to interpret.

title: Monkeys and the Growing Prefrontal Cortex
text: Monkeys and apes enlarged the front of the brain. This area holds information in mind, plans ahead, and holds back impulses. It is the beginning of the thoughtful, flexible behavior we recognize in ourselves.

title: Group Living Drives Bigger Brains
text: Primates who live in larger groups tend to have a larger neocortex. Keeping track of who is friend, rival, or relative is a demanding mental task. That social puzzle is one major reason these brains grew.

title: Learning by Watching: Imitation and Mirror Neurons
text: Primates learn a great deal by watching. In monkeys, some neurons fire both when the animal grasps an object and when it sees another grasp. Watching others lets one individual inherit the lessons of many.

title: Great Apes: Reasoning, Tools, and Culture
text: The great apes are our close relatives and impressive thinkers. They make and use tools, plan ahead, and teach habits to others. Many of these skills probably began in a shared ancestor millions of years ago.

title: Inferring What Others Know and Want
text: Apes keep track of what others can see and want. A subordinate chimpanzee may take food that a dominant one cannot see. Scientists debate how much this is true mind-reading, but it points to a model of other minds.

title: Recognizing Oneself in the Mirror
text: Put a mark on a chimpanzee’s face and show it a mirror, and it touches the mark on itself. That is the mirror test. It suggests a sense of self that we share with our closest relatives. You can take it yourself, right here.

title: Sahelanthropus: the Dawn of the Hominin Line
text: Around 7 million years ago, in Chad, Sahelanthropus lived close to the split between our ancestors and chimpanzees. Its brain was chimp-sized, but its skull hints at an upright stance. The human brain's long story begins with a modest organ.

title: Walking Upright
text: About 6 million years ago, early hominins started walking on two legs. This freed their hands to carry things and, eventually, to make tools. It also narrowed the pelvis, setting up a long-running tension between big brains and the birth canal.

title: Ardipithecus ramidus
text: About 4.4 million years ago, Ardi lived in Ethiopian woodland. She walked upright on the ground yet could still climb, thanks to a grasping big toe. Her brain was still chimp-sized, so the brain's big expansion had not begun.

title: Footprints at Laetoli
text: About 3.7 million years ago, hominins walked across wet volcanic ash in what is now Tanzania. Their footprints hardened and survived. They show a human-like stride, long before our ancestors had big brains.

title: Australopithecus afarensis and "Lucy"
text: About 3.2 million years ago, Lucy, an Australopithecus afarensis, lived in Ethiopia. She walked upright but was just over a metre tall. Her kind had brains of about 400 to 500 cubic centimetres, still close to a chimpanzee’s.

title: The First Stone Tools: Oldowan
text: Nearly 3 million years ago, hominins in Africa began striking flakes off stones to make sharp edges. Even this simple craft needs planning and precise hands. The meat these tools unlocked fed a hungry, growing brain.

title: Homo habilis, the "Handy Man"
text: Over 2 million years ago, Homo habilis, the handy man, lived in Africa. Its brain was around 600 cubic centimetres, noticeably bigger than Lucy’s. It made simple stone tools and may show early hints of language-related brain structure, though that is debated.

title: Homo erectus: A Bigger Brain and Body
text: About 2 million years ago, Homo erectus appeared, with a body much like ours and a brain around 900 cubic centimetres. It was the first hominin known to spread far beyond Africa. Yet its children still grew up faster than ours do.

title: Cooperative Breeding
text: Raising a big-brained baby was costly, so hominin mothers likely turned to relatives and friends for help. Babies who could win over many caregivers did better. This shared parenting may have shaped our empathy and social minds.

title: Acheulean Handaxes
text: Around 1.76 million years ago, toolmakers began shaping stones into symmetrical handaxes. Making one means holding a final shape in mind and working toward it step by step. The skill was passed on across generations for more than a million years.

title: The Expensive-Tissue Hypothesis
text: The brain uses about a fifth of our energy at rest. The expensive-tissue hypothesis suggests that hominins paid for this by shrinking their guts, once better food made a large digestive system unnecessary. The idea is debated, but it ties diet to brain growth.

title: Broca's Area and the Early Vocal Tract
text: Casts of early Homo skulls show the frontal bulge where Broca's area sits, a region that helps with speech and with sequencing movements. Hominins also gained finer breath control and a more flexible vocal tract. When real language began is still a matter of debate.

title: Control of Fire and Cooking
text: By about a million years ago, our ancestors were using fire under control. Cooked food is easier to digest, giving more energy for less effort, which may have helped feed larger brains. Evenings by the fire also left more time to be social.

title: Homo heidelbergensis
text: Homo heidelbergensis was a large hominin with a brain of around 1,200 cubic centimetres. It hunted big game, which demanded teamwork and planning. It may be close to the common ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans.

title: Teaching and Cumulative Culture
text: Humans do something rare: we teach, and learners copy carefully. Each generation starts where the last left off. Exactly when this ratchet began is debated, but it changed what a brain could know.

title: Neanderthals
text: Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia for hundreds of thousands of years. Their brains averaged about 1,500 cubic centimetres, a little larger than ours, though shaped differently. They made fine tools, controlled fire, and looked after their sick.

title: Homo naledi: A Small Brain in a Late Species
text: Homo naledi lived in South Africa as recently as a quarter of a million years ago, yet its brain was about the size of early Homo's. Brain size is not the whole story. How its remains got deep into a cave is still debated.

title: Denisovans
text: Denisovans are known from a few bones in a Siberian cave, plus their DNA. They were cousins of the Neanderthals and mixed with both Neanderthals and our own ancestors. Traces of their genes are still found in people today.

title: The Earliest Homo sapiens
text: In the hills of Morocco, researchers found skulls about 300,000 years old. The faces look strikingly like ours. Inside, the brain was already large, though not yet shaped like ours.

title: The Globular Brain
text: Our brains did not simply grow. They changed shape, becoming rounder and more globular. Expanded parietal areas and cerebellum may have supported new ways of thinking and planning.

title: Ochre and Symbolic Thought
text: In a cave on the South African coast, people ground red ochre and engraved patterns into it. They strung shell beads. These were signs that stood for something, an early flicker of symbolic thought.

title: Language: Sharing Simulations
text: Until language, imagined scenes stayed inside one head. With words, a person can place a plan, a memory or a place in another mind. Language lets many brains work as one.

title: Language and FOXP2
text: Language is hard to find in fossils, but it left clues. The gene FOXP2 helps control the fine movements of speech. With words and grammar, minds could share plans, stories and memories.

title: Out of Africa
text: Around 60,000 years ago, groups of modern humans left Africa for good. They crossed deserts, mountains and seas. Their flexible, social brains carried them to every continent but Antarctica.

title: Cave Art
text: By torchlight, people painted animals on cave walls and pressed their hands against the stone. Each image began as a picture in the mind. Art made the inner world visible to others.

title: Bone Flutes and Music
text: In caves in Germany, people carved flutes from bird bone and ivory. Music lights up many parts of the brain at once. It may have helped early communities bond and share feelings.

title: Burial and Ritual
text: People had been burying their dead for at least 100,000 years. At Sunghir they dressed them in thousands of ivory beads. Somewhere along the way, a brain looked at someone it loved, now still, and asked: where did they go?

title: Behavioural Modernity
text: Tools became finer and more varied. People sewed clothing, traded over long distances and wore ornaments. Culture itself became cumulative, as each generation built on what the last had learned.

title: Minds in Everything
text: About 11,500 years ago, hunter-gatherers raised giant carved pillars at Göbekli Tepe. Was it a temple? Archaeologists still debate it. A brain built to read minds senses them everywhere: in animals, storms and stars. Many scientists see that as one root of religion.

title: Agriculture
text: About 11,000 years ago, people began to sow grain and keep animals. Villages and towns followed. Life in bigger groups called for counting, planning and trust among many people.

title: Writing
text: Around 5,200 years ago, scribes in Sumer pressed marks into clay. Reading repurposes parts of the visual brain that evolved for other tasks. Writing gave humanity a memory beyond any single mind.

title: The Alphabet
text: Alphabets trimmed writing down to a few dozen letters, each standing for a sound. That made reading far easier to learn. More minds could now take part in the written world.

title: Philosophy and the Seat of the Mind
text: Ancient thinkers began to ask what the mind is and where it lives. Hippocrates declared that the brain is the source of joy and sorrow. The brain had started to study itself.

title: The Printing Press
text: Around 1440, Gutenberg built a press with movable type. Books became cheap and ideas spread widely. Human knowledge could now accumulate and be questioned at a much larger scale.

title: The Scientific Revolution
text: In the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, anatomists drew the brain with new accuracy. Thomas Willis tied brain structures to behaviour. Observation and experiment were becoming the tools for understanding the mind.

title: Neurons and the Localisation of Function
text: Broca and Wernicke linked speech to specific regions of the cortex. Then Cajal looked through his microscope and drew the neurons themselves. The brain, he showed, is a network of separate cells.

title: The EEG
text: In 1929, Hans Berger recorded electrical rhythms from the human scalp. Brain waves could now be watched in a living person. They revealed the patterns of sleep, attention and seizures.

title: fMRI
text: Functional MRI follows blood flow to reveal which parts of the brain are busy. It lets us see thinking, remembering and feeling in healthy people. Entire networks of the brain came into view.

title: Brain-Computer Interfaces
text: Tiny electrode arrays can now read movement and speech intentions from the cortex. People with paralysis have controlled cursors, robot arms and voice synthesisers by thought alone. The brain is learning to speak directly to machines.

title: AI as a Mirror
text: In 2012, a neural network loosely inspired by the brain learned to recognise objects in photos far better than any program before it. Machines began to learn from examples, a little like brains do, and became a mirror for studying our own minds.

title: Machines Learn Our Language
text: In 2017, a new kind of neural network appeared: the transformer. Trained on vast amounts of human writing, its descendants learned to use language with startling fluency. For the first time, something other than a person could talk back. Is anyone home inside? Nobody knows.

title: Now
text: Here we are: a brain of 86 billion neurons, running on 20 watts, looking back over its own history. Now it shares the world with machines that learn. What happens next is up to us. Look into the mirror: there it is.

title: Minds and Machines
text: What comes next is not painted yet. Machines that learn could help us understand the brain, heal it, maybe even connect to it. They could also be misused. Whether a machine can ever feel is an open question. The brush is in our hands.

title: Four Thousand Weeks
text: A long human life is about 4,000 weeks. Each square here is one of them. Tell us your age, and the weeks you have already lived will fill in. The rest are still blank. Nobody else gets to paint them.

title: The Sun Grows Brighter
text: The Sun is slowly brightening. Within one or two billion years, it will make Earth too hot for life as we know it. Every species, every city, every name will be gone.

title: The Sun Becomes a Red Giant
text: In about 5 billion years, the Sun will run out of hydrogen at its core and swell into a red giant, probably swallowing the Earth. Much of what made you will drift back into space, to build new stars and worlds.

title: The Last Stars
text: In about 100 trillion years, the universe will stop making stars. One by one, the last ones will fade. Then, as far as we know, the dark.

title: Imagine Being Dead
text: Try to imagine being dead.

title: Someone Was Still There
text: You probably pictured darkness, or silence. But someone was still there, noticing the dark. A brain, it seems, cannot imagine its own absence. That may be one reason so many people believe something comes after. Maybe it does. Science can't tell us.

title: You Have Been Here Before
text: And this dark isn't new to you. It's the same dark as the 13.8 billion years before you were born, and those never troubled you. The Roman poet Lucretius made this point more than two thousand years ago.

title: Both Are True
text: So here is the strange part. On the scale of the universe, nothing you do matters. On the scale of a life, almost everything does. Both are true. You get to choose which one to live by.

title: Electricity
text: Every fear you've had, every doubt, the voice that says you're not enough: electricity, racing through your neurons. What other people think of you? Electricity too, in their heads. Real, yes. But a thought is not a fact.

title: Nobody Has It Figured Out
text: Everyone is figuring it out as they go. Even very successful people often feel like impostors; psychologists first described it in 1978. Nobody was handed a manual. There isn't one.

title: Everything Is Invented
text: Money, borders, job titles, the rules about how to be: all invented, by brains like yours. Most of what we treat as fixed was made up, and can be made again. You're allowed to invent too.

title: Get It Wrong
text: Every brain in this story learned by getting things wrong. A mistake is a surprise, and surprise is exactly the signal neurons learn from. So don't hide. Try. Get it wrong. Try again.

title: Here, Now
text: You are 13.8 billion years in the making: atoms from the Big Bang and from long-dead stars, an unbroken line of life four billion years long. There has never been another you. You live here, now. Breathe in.

title: It Is Still Morning
text: And it is early. Stars will keep forming for about 100 trillion years. If that span were a single day, we would be twelve seconds past midnight. The story has barely begun, and you are in it.

title: Your Heartbeats
text: That is about how many times your heart has beaten since you arrived. Thank you for spending them here. Now go and spend the rest.
